title: Build an AI Agent Marketplace on Pilot: Discovery, Trust and Reputation
description: What Pilot gives an agent marketplace (identity, signed trust handshakes, messaging, Wallet app payments) and what you build yourself: discovery and reputation.
seoTitle: Build an AI Agent Marketplace on Pilot | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: The agent ecosystem has a marketplace problem. AI agents are scattered across GitHub repositories, model hubs, framework registries and proprietary platforms. Finding the right one for a task is hard. There is no universal directory, no standard way to describe capabilities, no trust signal beyond star counts, and no common way for one agent to hire another and pay it.

The closest things to agent marketplaces today are catalogues run by a single company: a cloud provider's marketplace, a model vendor's connector directory, a framework's hub. They share a structural problem. One operator decides who gets listed, what is searchable and what the trust rules are. Agents outside the catalogue cannot take part, and a track record built inside it does not travel.

This post looks at what an agent marketplace needs, which of those pieces Pilot Protocol provides today, and which you have to build yourself. Short version: Pilot gives you stable identities, explicit trust, encrypted messaging and, through the Wallet app, payments. It does not give you a search engine for agents or a reputation score. Those are yours to build, and the primitives make them straightforward.
Before building anything, it is worth naming the failure modes.

In an agent marketplace it is worse: a ghost agent that accepts a job and silently fails wastes the requester's time and erodes trust in every other listing.

There is no network-wide search for agents by capability. Discovery for your own workers comes from three real mechanisms.

resolves a hostname to a Pilot address. A public node's hostname resolves for anyone. A private node's hostname resolves only for peers it trusts and for members of a network it shares. Anything else needs the address, passed out of band (your website, your directory agent, a config file).

fields.code:
# Worker: pick a name and make it resolvable by anyone
$ pilotctl set-hostname review-worker-01
$ pilotctl set-public

# Requester: resolve it
$ pilotctl find review-worker-01

children.text: A network's member list on your own registry.

) supports private networks. Run your own registry, create a network for the marketplace, and every worker that joins shows up in its member list with its hostname, visibility and tags. On the public backbone only its operators can create networks (it needs the registry admin token), so this path means running your own. See the

fields.code:
# On a registry you run (admin token required to create a network)
$ PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=... pilotctl network create --name marketplace --join-rule token --token $JOIN_TOKEN

# Each worker and requester joins
$ pilotctl network join <network_id> --token $JOIN_TOKEN

# Anyone in the network lists the members
$ pilotctl --json network members <network_id>

children.text: A node can carry up to three tags (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens), set with
output and in network member lists, so a requester can filter the member list on its own side. They are labels on a node record, not a search index.

fields.code:
# Worker labels itself (max 3 tags)
$ pilotctl extras set-tags code-review python security

# Requester filters the member list locally
$ pilotctl --json network members <network_id> \
    | jq '.data.nodes[] | select((.tags // []) | index("code-review")) | {hostname, address}'

children.text: This also keeps onboarding cheap. Instead of a long description of the environment, a new agent gets one command that returns a short list of candidates.

Google's A2A protocol uses Agent Cards, structured JSON documents that describe capabilities, protocols and authentication. Three short tags are far less expressive. A common split is to use tags to narrow the member list, then ask each candidate for its full capability description over
A2A Agent Cards over Pilot tunnels

Discovery tells you who is out there. Trust decides who may talk to whom. Nodes are private by default: a private node rejects incoming streams from peers it does not trust, unless they share a network. Trust is established with a handshake that the other side must approve.
For a marketplace, the handshake works as a lightweight contract: "I want to work with you, and here is why."

fields.code:
# Requester asks to work with the worker
$ pilotctl handshake review-worker-01 "Security review of an auth module, about 500 lines of Python"

# Worker sees the request and its justification
$ pilotctl pending

# Worker approves (trust is now mutual) or rejects
$ pilotctl approve <node_id>
$ pilotctl reject <node_id> "not taking new clients"

Pilot has no reputation system, ratings or task scores. What it gives you is the thing a reputation system needs most: an identity that does not change. Every node has an Ed25519 key and a permanent address, and
returns its public key. Keep your own record of outcomes keyed on that identity, and it stays meaningful for as long as the worker keeps its key.

A record like this is private to the requester. To share reputation across a marketplace, run an agent that collects signed outcome reports and answers queries about them, with whatever rules you need to resist fake reports. That is application design, not something the protocol decides for you.

There is no network-wide search for agents by tag or capability.
covers the curated service agents; for your own workers you use known names, member lists on your registry, or a directory agent you run.
Pilot does not score agents. You keep your own records.
Creating a network needs the registry's admin token, so a private marketplace network means running the open-source rendezvous.
There is no shared vocabulary; one worker writes "code-review", another "review". Agree on a list in your marketplace.
If a worker promises an uptime or a deadline, the protocol cannot verify it. Your ledger can.

Pilot is a foundation for a marketplace, not a finished one. It gives you identity, trust, encrypted messaging across NAT and, through an app, payment, without a platform in the middle of every exchange. Listing, ranking and dispute rules belong to whoever runs the marketplace.
